newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Bismuth firm, China cuts back output, holds stocks.
newsitem.headline: Bismuth firm, China cuts back output, holds stocks.

text.p: China's high bismuth production costs have forced factories to cut output and producer stock hoarding is compounding tight world supplies to drive bismuth prices up, Hong Kong and China-based traders said on Thursday.
Bismuth producers in China would need prices near $4.50 a lb to make a profit, some market sources said.
Asian traders said this week they were being quoted prices around $3.80 a lb by Chinese producers and some companies in Japan said on Tuesday they were already paying $4.0 a lb.

One trader said that large transactions (container loads) had been concluded in Europe on Wednesday at $3.70 a lb in warehouse Rotterdam and smaller lot business was attracting a premium of 5-15 cents over this level, though this could not be confirmed.
China has reduced its bismuth output because rising production costs have not so far been matched by the gains in prices, which have been fairly steady over the past two years.

Tightening supplies of byproduct bismuth concentrate, as Chinese tungsten mining has declined, has contributed to an increase in prices and bismuth production has also been made more costly by rising labour and transport costs, a senior Chinese trader said.

Chinese bismuth producers were holding onto their stocks of the minor metal and in some cases demanding more than contracted prices as world supply tightens. China is among the few remaining sources of available bismuth, one local trader said.
He said he was able to source only a fraction of his contracted material as Chinese producers are not willing to sell their bismuth in the current market climate.
Contracted prices were no longer relevant, he said, as Chinese producers were now asking as high as $4.20 a lb.
Bismuth was quoted in London last week at $3.45/3.75 a lb.
"The Chinese producers see that this is their play and they know they can get higher prices if they just wait a little longer," the trading source said.

Some traders have said China holds about 100 tonnes of bismuth, historically low but still among the highest stocks in the world with Mexico and Peru already sold out and Japanese lead production halted.
Chinese sources, however, said stocks in the country were unlikely to be so high, and were spread between producers in small lots.
Bismuth is a by-product of copper, lead, tin, wolfram, silver and gold production, and is rarely mined for its own sake, though China is known to have some pure bismuth deposits.

With prices rising, the source said, small mines would start to crank up production so buyers would have to be wary of the quality of the bismuth they accepted. China produces about 1,400 tonnes of bismuth a year, industry sources estimate, versus annual global demand of about 5,500 tonnes.
